title: Why ChatGPT for Teachers Might Make Things Worse
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Carl Hendrick tests OpenAI's new ChatGPT for Teachers tool and concludes that its central promise -- decomposing curriculum content into discrete, atomised pieces for AI-assisted planning -- can actively undermine subjects whose value depends on narrative coherence and interpretive flow rather than isolated facts. He argues that history, literature, and philosophy lose exactly what makes them worth teaching when broken into disconnected 'facts' about dates or literary devices: the causal relationships, the narrative arc, the aesthetic encounter. Hendrick is careful not to dismiss atomisation wholesale -- he acknowledges the well-established cognitive-science case for retrieval practice, spacing, and interleaving, and grants that coordinating those principles precisely across thirty students and a full academic year is exactly the kind of logistical puzzle AI is well suited to help with. His worry is sharper than a blanket 'AI bad' critique: ChatGPT for Teachers risks not just failing to solve the wrong problems, but making the right problems -- actually implementing what we already know about learning -- even harder to solve if teachers offload judgment about what should and shouldn't be atomised to a tool that can't distinguish a procedural skill from an interpretive one.
points: Hendrick's central distinction is between content that decomposes well (procedural mechanisms, worked examples) and content that doesn't (historical narrative, literary interpretation, philosophical argument) -- atomisation destroys the latter's coherence.

He grants the cognitive-science case for retrieval practice, spaced repetition, and interleaving is well-established, and that coordinating those principles precisely for 30 students across a year is a genuine 'coordination puzzle at which AI excels and humans struggle.'

His sharpest warning is that the tool may make already-hard problems harder: 'it may make the right problems... even harder to solve' if it papers over the judgment calls about what should never be atomised in the first place.
The critique lands as a caution against reflexive adoption of a major AI vendor's new teacher-facing product rather than a wholesale rejection of AI-assisted planning.
quotes: There’s a predictable pattern when some edtech companies enter education: they build sophisticated solutions to problems that don’t exist while ignoring the problems real teachers actually face.

The notion that students can be taught “general critical thinking skills” to evaluate AI outputs represents a profound misunderstanding of how critical thinking actually works. Critical thinking is not a portable skill that operates independently of domain knowledge, it is the product of domain expertise.

When you decompose a historical period into disconnected “facts” about dates and events, you lose the causal relationships, the narrative coherence. When you break a poem into atomic elements like “metaphor,” “imagery,” and “tone,” you end up feature-spotting and destroy the aesthetic encounter that gives literature its power.

We know from decades of research that retrieval practice, spaced repetition, and interleaving produce robust learning gains. We know that there’s an optimal difficulty zone. We know that spacing intervals should dynamically adjust based on individual mastery.

The problem isn’t knowing these principles work; it’s implementing them with precision for thirty students simultaneously across multiple topics over an entire academic year. This is exactly the kind of coordination puzzle at which AI excels and humans struggle.

The issue isn’t just that ChatGPT for Teachers solves the wrong problems; it’s that in doing so, it may make the right problems (such as implementing what we actually know about how learning happens), even harder to solve.
